agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: Number words aren't the weakness: they're retrieved at 0.776, the same as digits. The weak `othernum` subclasses are derived quantities (0.582) and unit constants (0.587), which are implicit mental arithmetic. A third opener doesn't look natural either: "Okay" has 0.05% probability and everything else is around 1e-5, so forcing one would be a large push that repairs no identified failure. I'll set that aside. A more useful idea came out of the E2 result: boosting the retrieval head hurt result digits, which suggests attention affects arithmetic and that heads compete there. Arithmetic also matters more than the crude bound implied, because a per-step error compounds across about 3.3 steps. If per-step accuracy rose from 88% to 95%, solved problems would increase by about 29%, which is roughly +5 points. So I'll analyse arithmetic the way I analysed retrieval: from the same stored attention data, I'll find which heads attend to the operands when predicting result digits, separately for first and later digits, with the share landing on the correct operands. I'll also recompute the true per-equation error rates per operator, deduplicated and on finished answers only. If a specific head attends to operands at result tokens, that's the next circuit to test.

This is the sharpest finding yet, in two parts. First, layer 17 contains a separate operand circuit: at result digits, heads h2 and h3 put 0.59-0.62 of their attention on the equation's operands with peak hit rates of 0.76-0.85, and h1 does the same for first digits only. So L17 h0 retrieves numbers from the problem, while h1-h3 read the operands. That also explains why boosting h0 hurt result digits: the output is RMS-normalised, so its boost took share from the operand heads. Second, arithmetic error isn't uniform at all. It's 3% for small two-factor products and 11% for small two-term sums, but 25-70% for three-term sums and 79% for four-term sums. Long sums are a specific failure, and they tend to be the final step that sets the answer. The operand heads might be covering only some of the terms. Three things come next. I'll check whether wrong sums equal a partial sum of the terms, which would show dropped operands. I'll build an arithmetic screening set from the model's own contexts, with corrected results, so I can measure each operator and term-count class. Then I'll run a new baseline on that set, because future edits need a paired reference. If wrong sums often equal partial sums, then operand coverage is the mechanism and attention-based edits have a clear target.

Wrong multi-term sums are partly a coverage failure: 30 of 66 equal a partial sum of the terms, and in 22 of those 30 the dropped term is at the end, so the model stops adding too soon. The rest are off by tens or units, more like carry slips. The value of fixing this is measurable. Among finished failed answers, 45 end on a wrong multi-term sum and 39 on a wrong two-term equation. At the success rate of similar answers with correct final equations, that's a few points. So it's bounded but real, and it's a clean target. The screening set is ready: 450 reference texts plus 561 own-answer contexts with corrected results, 136 of them ending on a corrected wrong equation and 148 with multi-term sums. No edits are active, so this pass sets the baseline that later arithmetic candidates are compared against. There's nothing to confirm yet. It will give the per-class digit accuracy with correct prefixes, which should show multi-term sums as far weaker than two-term ones if the generation statistics reflect a real ability limit.

Now I'll index the arithmetic events: map each equation's result to token positions, keeping only those whose tokens match the digits exactly. Then I'll compute baseline accuracy per class (operator, number of terms, operand size), both per digit and per whole result, plus the accuracy on the subset where the model originally erred. This provides the reference for screening. If multi-term sums come out far weaker than two-term ones even with correct prefixes, the generation statistics reflect a real ability limit and not noise. Accuracy on originally-wrong equations also shows how much room an edit has: I'd expect it to be very low, because those are cases where greedy got it wrong.
